title: Explaining how
job: Steps and instructions in order, and what they are for
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE GERUND ARRIVES, AND L3-M2 NAMED IT AS MISSING WHILE WRITING ad labōrem eō. A gerund is a VERB USED AS A NOUN: ad legendum, ad scrībendum, ad discendum — 'for reading', 'for writing', 'for learning'. It takes the object shape after ad like any noun, so a purpose needs no clause at all. L3-M4's ut plus a subjunctive is the other way and both are correct: the gerund is tighter and can take no object, the clause can. A plain infinitive after ad is not an option — an infinitive has no case for a preposition to govern, which is why the gerund exists.

THE GERUNDIVE IS HOW LATIN SAYS 'SHOULD', AND IT AGREES. liber legendus est is 'the book is to-be-read', hence 'the book should be read' — legendus for a masculine thing, legenda for a feminine, legendum for a neuter. That is L2-M3's agreement on a new kind of word, and L2-M8's frāctus est was the same arrangement. Latin's 'should' carries the gender of what should be done, which no English speaker will expect.

THE GERUND AND THE GERUNDIVE ARE ONE ENDING APART AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT WORDS. ad legendum is a noun; legendum est is an adjective with nothing to agree with. Both are -ndum. After ad it is ALWAYS -ndum because a gerund has nothing to agree with; as a gerundive it moves to match. With no subject and no object at all the gerundive goes neuter and means 'one must' — legendum est, 'one must read' — which is how Latin states a rule with nobody in it, exactly as L3-M7's melius est gave advice with nobody in it.

A SET OF STEPS COSTS NO NEW GRAMMAR: prīmum lege, deinde scrībe, postrēmō dā. L2-M10's four sequencing adverbs plus L2-M5's imperative shape, and that is the whole of it — which is what leaves this module's cap free for the two -nd- forms. Instructions move freely between an imperative (accipe, 'take!') and an obligation (signandum est, 'it must be signed'), exactly as English moves between 'take' and 'it must be signed'.

BOTH WAYS OF SAYING PURPOSE IN ONE SENTENCE, ON PURPOSE: ad discendum lege, ut linguam discās. The gerund is two words and takes no object; the clause has a verb and can take one. A learner who has only the clause will write four words where two would do, and a learner who has only the gerund cannot say what they are learning.

cum IS 'WITH' HERE AND IT HAS A SECOND READING COMING. L1-M7 owns this key for cum plus the ablative — cum magistrō, cum stilō — and M6 of this level opens cum plus a SUBJUNCTIVE meaning 'when'. Same four letters, same key in the index, two grammars. This module's cum is a tool or a person and nothing else, and its note says the other reading is coming, because when it arrives the note will be the only place the two can be told apart.

sentences.cue: I am coming in order to read.

words.note: 'For', with the object shape after it — and a gerund takes that shape like any noun. L1-M4's preposition doing a job it has not done before.
'Reading' — and ONE key for two words: a GERUND (a noun) after ad, and a GERUNDIVE (an adjective) in legendum est, 'one must read'. Same four letters; the frame decides.
'I come': veniō, venīs, venit, venīmus, venīre.

sentences.trap: L3-M2 said purpose was ad plus a plain noun and named the gerund as missing. Here it is: legendum is the verb legō turned into a noun, so ad legendum is 'for reading' with no clause in it at all. L3-M4's ut plus a subjunctive is the other way and needs a verb; this needs none.

words.note: 'First of all'. L2-M10's adverb, at the front of its clause.
'Read!' — legō's order shape. L2-M5's bibe and L1-M8's dā are the same kind of word, and a set of steps is built out of them.
'Next'. L2-M10's sequencer, at the front of its clause.
'Write!' — scrībō's order shape. Same pattern as lege and as L2-M5's bibe.

sentences.trap: A set of steps costs no new grammar at all. L2-M10 gave the sequencing adverbs and L2-M5 the imperative, so instructions are built entirely out of the ladder — which is what leaves this module's cap free for the two -nd- shapes.

mistake.why: infinitives where imperatives belong. An infinitive names an action and an imperative orders one, so this reads as a list of activities rather than a set of steps — and L2-M5 established that Latin instructs with bare commands.

sentences.display: Ad discendum lege, ut linguam discās.
sentences.cue: Read in order to learn, so that you learn the language.
sentences.literal: for learning read! so-that language you-may-learn

words.note: 'For', with the object shape after it.
'For learning' — a gerund, L3-M2's discō turned into a noun. ad discendum is 'for the purpose of learning'.
'Read!' — legō's order shape. L2-M5's bibe and L1-M8's dā are the same kind of word, and a set of steps is built out of them.
'So that' — with a subjunctive. L3-M4's word, and the purpose reading only.
'Language' as the thing learned. L3-M2's word.
'That you may learn' — the present subjunctive of discō. L3-M4's mood, and scrībās is scrībō in the same mood: the ending is the same on every verb.

sentences.trap: Both purposes in one sentence, on purpose. ad discendum is tight and has no verb; ut linguam discās has a verb and can take an object. That is the whole difference between the two, and a sentence with one of each is the only way to show it.
sentences.sound: ad dis-CEN-dum LE-ge, ut LIN-guam dis-CĀS. The -cen- and the -cās- are the same verb, two shapes apart.

mistake.display: Ad discendum lege, ut linguam discere.
mistake.why: an infinitive inside the purpose clause. ut needs a subjunctive, which L3-M4 settled, and the presence of a gerund earlier in the sentence makes an author reach for another verbal noun instead of a mood.

'To be written' — the gerundive of scrībō, agreeing: scrībendus, scrībenda, scrībendum. That last shape is ALSO the gerund, ad scrībendum: one key, two words.

sentences.trap: The gerundive is feminine here because epistula is, and the obligation has not changed at all. Latin's 'should' carries the gender of what should be done, which no English speaker will expect and which is the one thing that makes these forms feel strange rather than merely new.

sentences.display: Prīmum chartam accipe, deinde signandum est.
sentences.cue: First take the form, then it must be signed.
sentences.literal: first form take! next to-be-signed it-is

words.note: 'First of all'. L2-M10's adverb.
'Form, paper' — a Greek loan with a plain a. L3-M8's word.
'Take!' — the order shape of L2-M7's accipiō. accipiō, accipit, accipiam, accipe.
'Next'. L2-M10's sequencer.
'It is to-be-signed' — the gerundive of L3-M8's signō with nothing to agree with, so neuter.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: An imperative and an obligation in one set of steps, and they are not the same thing. accipe tells you to do it; signandum est says it has to be done, by whoever. Instructions in Latin move between the two freely, and English does the same with 'take' and 'it must be signed'.
sentences.sound: PRĪ-mum CHAR-tam AC-ci-pe, DE-in-de sig-NAN-dum EST. Twelve syllables, and the two halves are an order and a rule.

mistake.why: the masculine ending where nothing is being agreed with. There is no noun for signandum to answer to — the form is impersonal — so an -us invents a masculine subject the sentence does not have.

words.note: 'For', with the object shape after it.
'For writing' — a GERUND here, the noun, after ad. The word three places later is the other kind.
'Pen' as the subject — stilō after cum. A pointed iron for writing on wax.
'To be bought' — the GERUNDIVE of L1-M8's emō, agreeing with stilus and so masculine: emendus, emenda, emendum.
